title: When Should You Sell a Stock You Own?
summary: How to decide when to sell a stock: the good reasons, the emotional traps to avoid, the tax to expect, and how selling works on the NGX.
body_markdown:
**In short:** Sell a stock for a sound reason, not because the price dipped. Good reasons include the reason you bought it no longer holding, the company’s fundamentals weakening, needing the money, or rebalancing your portfolio. The costliest mistake is panic-selling on short-term falls. Selling can also trigger tax. This is general information, not advice.


Most investing advice tells you what to buy. Far less of it tells you when to let go, which is strange, because selling well is at least as hard as buying well and arguably matters more. The decision to sell is where fear and greed do their worst damage, and where a good investment can quietly turn into a poor outcome.


This guide walks through when it makes sense to sell a stock, the reasons that usually cost people money, the tax to keep in mind, and how selling actually works on the NGX. It is general information, not investment advice, and it recommends no particular action on any stock. If you are still deciding what to buy in the first place, our[guide to choosing NGX stocks](https://learn.investbamboo.com/how-to-choose-nigerian-stocks-a-beginners-guide/) is the companion to this one, and our[complete guide to investing in the Nigerian stock market](https://learn.investbamboo.com/how-to-invest-in-the-nigerian-stock-market-ngx-a-complete-beginners-guide/) covers the basics.


## When should you sell a stock?


You should sell when there is a sound, considered reason to, not because the price moved against you for a few days. There is no perfect formula, and even seasoned investors treat it as judgement rather than a rule. But the good reasons to sell tend to fall into a short, recognisable list, and so do the bad ones.


The rest of this guide takes both. Getting clear on which is which, before you are staring at a falling price and feeling the urge to act, is most of the battle.


## Good reasons to sell


The soundest reasons to sell share a common thread: something about the investment or your own circumstances has genuinely changed, not just the daily price.


**The reason you bought it no longer holds.** Every purchase should rest on a thesis, a simple story about why you expected the company to do well. If that story breaks, for example the company keeps missing its numbers, loses its competitive edge, or changes direction in a way you no longer believe in, the original reason to own it is gone. Holding on only because you have already put money and time in is a trap.


**The fundamentals have deteriorated.** If the business itself is weakening, with falling profits, mounting debt, or a market turning against it, that is a signal to reassess, as our companion guide on assessing a company explains.


**The stock has become significantly overvalued.** If a share price has run far ahead of what the business realistically earns, some investors trim or exit. Judging this is difficult and imprecise, so it is a reason to think, not an automatic trigger.


**You need the money.** A perfectly valid reason. If you are approaching a goal you were investing for, or your circumstances have changed, selling to meet a real need is sensible, not a failure.


**You are rebalancing.** If one stock has grown to dominate your portfolio, selling some of it to spread your money more evenly is a way to manage risk, not a verdict on the company.


**The company is being acquired.** When a company agrees to be bought, its share price usually moves close to the agreed price, and how you respond depends on the terms.


## The reasons that cost people money


Now the other list, the reasons that feel urgent in the moment and tend to destroy returns over time, and that rank among the[common mistakes investors make](https://learn.investbamboo.com/common-mistakes-new-nigerian-investors-make-and-how-to-avoid-them/) . Almost all of them come down to reacting to price rather than to fundamentals.


The biggest is[panic-selling during a market fall](https://learn.investbamboo.com/what-happens-to-your-investments-in-a-market-downturn/) . When prices drop sharply, the instinct to sell and stop the pain is powerful, but acting on it usually means locking in a loss and missing the recovery. Nigerian analysts made exactly this point during the 2026 market correction. As[Nairametrics noted at the time](https://nairametrics.com/2026/06/27/ngx-correction-why-smart-investors-arent-panicking/) , too many investors buy on rumours, social media excitement, or fear of missing out, then panic when prices begin to fall, while disciplined investors stay focused on the quality of the businesses they own and the long-term value those investments can generate.


Other costly reasons include selling on a scary headline before understanding whether it actually affects your company, selling out of boredom because a stock has gone nowhere for a while, and selling a solid holding to chase whatever is spiking elsewhere. There is also the classic error the investor Peter Lynch warned about: selling your winners quickly to lock in a small gain while clinging to your losers hoping they recover, which is the opposite of what tends to build wealth.


## The emotional trap, and how to avoid it


Selling is where emotion does the most harm, because a falling price triggers fear and a rising one triggers greed, and both push you toward decisions you would not make calmly. Recognising that is the first defence.


The antidote is not to feel nothing, which is impossible, but to decide your reasons in advance and judge the business rather than the price ticker. A price falling does not, by itself, mean anything is wrong with the company. Markets move on sentiment, profit-taking, interest rates, and broad economic news, often with little to do with the specific businesses you own. During the 2026 correction, much of the selling was profit-taking and portfolio rebalancing rather than a sign that the underlying companies had become bad investments.


So when you feel the urge to sell, pause and ask a simple question: has the business actually changed, or has only the price changed? If it is only the price, that is usually a reason to wait, not to act.


## What about tax when you sell?


Selling shares can have tax consequences, so it is worth knowing before you act rather than after. In Nigeria, capital gains on shares are taxed, though an exemption covers most retail investors, and the rules changed in 2026. Rather than summarise it loosely here, our[guide to tax on Nigerian stocks](https://learn.investbamboo.com/tax-on-nigerian-stocks-what-ngx-investors-need-to-know/) explains how gains are taxed and who is exempt. The short version is that most small investors are exempt, but it is worth checking your position before selling a large holding.


## How selling actually works on the NGX


Selling a stock on the NGX is mechanically simple: you place a sell order through your broker or investing platform, and once it matches with a buyer, the sale goes through and the proceeds settle to your account. On[Bamboo](https://investbamboo.com/nigerian-stocks) , you can sell your Nigerian shares from the same app you used to buy them, at any time the market is open.


One recent change worth knowing: since 1 June 2026, the NGX settles trades on a T+1 basis, meaning a completed sale settles one business day after the trade, rather than the longer wait that used to apply. That gets your money back to you faster once you have decided to sell.


## Building a simple selling discipline


The best protection against bad selling decisions is to decide your rules before you are emotional. A few habits help. Write down your reason for buying each stock, so you have something to check against later when you wonder whether to sell. Review your holdings on a schedule, perhaps quarterly, rather than reacting to every daily move. And separate the two questions that get tangled in the heat of the moment: is this a good business, and is now the time I need the money. As[personal finance guidance on selling](https://www.kiplinger.com/investing/how-to-decide-to-sell-a-stock-a-master-guide) puts it, there are few hard-and-fast rules, and deciding when to sell is more art than science, which is exactly why having your own criteria set in advance matters so much.


None of this removes the difficulty. But an investor with a written thesis and a review schedule makes far calmer, better selling decisions than one staring at a red screen deciding in the moment.


## Frequently asked questions


**When is the right time to sell a stock?** When there is a sound reason: the reason you bought it no longer holds, the company’s fundamentals have weakened, the stock is significantly overvalued, you need the money, or you are rebalancing. A falling price on its own is usually not a good enough reason.


**Should I sell when the market is falling?** Usually not, if nothing has changed about the companies you own. Panic-selling during a fall tends to lock in losses and miss the recovery. Ask whether the business has changed or only the price has, and if it is only the price, waiting is often wiser.


**Do I pay tax when I sell shares in Nigeria?** Capital gains on shares are taxed, but an exemption covers most retail investors, and the rules changed in 2026. Check your position before selling a large holding. Our tax guide covers the detail.


**How do I sell a stock on the NGX?** You place a sell order through your broker or investing app, and once it matches with a buyer, the sale completes and the proceeds settle to your account. On the NGX, trades now settle one business day after the trade.


**How do I avoid selling at the wrong time?** Decide your reasons for selling in advance, write down why you bought each stock, review on a schedule rather than daily, and judge the business rather than the price. This keeps emotion from driving the decision.
